big: Lose 50% and you need 100% to get back. The maths of losses is lopsided, and it is the reason a smoother fund can end richer than a more exciting one with the same average return.

lines: My small cap fund went up 50% one year and fell 50% the next. Plus 50 and minus 50 average to zero, so I should be at ₹100 still, right?
Good guess, and a very common one. Put ₹100 in and watch it move, one year at a time.

alt: Three bars: 100 rupees, then 150 after a 50 percent rise, then 75 after a 50 percent fall
caps: Now a 50% fall. Half of ₹150 is ₹75, not ₹50.
The average of +50% and -50% is zero. The money ended 25% lower.

alt: Four pairs of bars comparing a fall with the gain needed to recover it
caps: A 10% fall needs an 11.1% gain to get back to where you were.
A 20% fall needs 25%. A one-third fall needs 50%.
A 50% fall needs a 100% gain. Money has to double just to break even.
The deeper the fall, the more the recovery costs. Small falls are cheap to repair.

alt: Two lines: a steady 10 percent a year and a path that alternates plus 40 and minus 20 percent
caps: Both paths have an average return of 10% a year. One is steady. One alternates +40% and -20%.
The jumpy one looks faster in the good years. It is ahead after year 1.
But every fall takes a bigger bite out of a bigger pile.
After 10 years: ₹100 became ₹259 on the steady path and ₹176 on the jumpy one.

note: Growth per year is the square root of 1.4 times 0.8, minus one. The gap is called volatility drag. The bigger the swings, the larger it gets.

q: A client's ₹1 lakh portfolio falls 40%, to ₹60,000. What gain does it need to get back to ₹1 lakh?
opts: 40%, because the climb back has to match the fall exactly
60%, because it now holds sixty percent of its old value
80%, because falls count double on the way back up again
why: A 40% gain on ₹60,000 is only ₹24,000. It leaves the portfolio at ₹84,000, still short of ₹1 lakh.
A 60% gain adds ₹36,000 and lands at ₹96,000. That is still ₹4,000 short of ₹1 lakh.
An 80% gain overshoots, giving ₹1,08,000. The exact answer is ₹40,000 over ₹60,000.
The gain is measured on the smaller base. ₹40,000 divided by ₹60,000 is 66.7%, more than the 40% fall.

q: Fund A earned 12% in each of four years. Fund B earned +40%, -16%, +40%, -16%, which also averages 12%. After four years of ₹1 lakh in each, which statement is true?
opts: The two end equal, because their average yearly return is the same
A ends higher, near ₹1,57,000 against about ₹1,38,000 for B
B ends higher, because its good years were bigger than any year of A
B ends higher, but only because two of its years were falls instead of three
why: Equal averages do not give equal endings. Growth compounds, so the order and size of swings changes the result.
A: 1.12 four times is about 1.57. B: 1.4 times 0.84, twice, is about 1.38. Swings reduce the ending value.
B's falls did more harm than its +40% years did good. Compounded, B ends lower than A.
B had two falls and two gains, but each fall hit a larger pile. The count of years is not the point.

q: A client says she would rather catch every rally than avoid big falls. A market goes +40% then -30%. A fund captures 70% of each rise and 50% of each fall. Where does ₹100 end in the fund?
opts: About ₹109, since it rises 28% to ₹128 and then falls 15%
About ₹113, since 28 less 15 is 13, so ₹100 gains ₹13 in total
About ₹98, since the fund follows the market and ends where it does
Exactly ₹100, because the rises and the falls are of similar size
why: ₹100 times 1.28 is ₹128. A 15% fall takes it to ₹108.8. The market itself ended near ₹98.
Returns multiply, they do not add. The 15% fall acts on ₹128, a bigger base than ₹100.
The fund took only part of each move. It did not copy the market, so it did not end at ₹98.
The rise and fall are not equal. The fund gains 28% and loses 15%, so it ends above ₹100.

q: An adviser argues that avoiding big falls matters more than catching every rally. What is the reason?
opts: Rallies in the market are always smaller than the falls that follow them in time
Avoiding falls removes the tax on the gains that a portfolio would otherwise earn
A deep fall needs a bigger gain to repair, so small falls leave more to compound
A fall of 50% needs only a 50% gain to bring the money back up to the start
why: Rallies are not always smaller. The point is the arithmetic of recovery, whatever the sizes are.
Tax is on gains when you redeem. A smaller fall does not cancel tax on the gains that you make.
Falls compound against you: 50% down needs 100% up. Cutting the fall leaves more rupees to grow later.
That has the maths backwards. After a 50% fall the money must double, a 100% gain, to break even.

pts: A 20% fall needs a 25% gain. A 50% fall needs 100%. Recovery is steeper than the fall.
Plus 50% then minus 50% leaves ₹75, not ₹100. Two paths with the same average return can end far apart.
The less volatile path ends richer. That arithmetic is the core of the multi-asset case.
